newsitem.title: GERMANY: German police uncover more of tsar's treasure.
newsitem.headline: German police uncover more of tsar's treasure.

text.p: Police said on Thursday they had found a chest of drawers that probably belonged to Russia's Amber Chamber, a long lost treasure stolen by Nazi German troops in World War Two.
Police, who last week found a mosaic they were confident belonged to the priceless Tsarist treasure, said the chest would be examined to check its authenticity.

If the new find, a lacquered wooden chest inlaid with floral patterns, really belonged to the assembly of amber wall panels and furniture presented to the Russian tsars by Prussia in 1712, it would have stood directly below the mosaic found last week, police said.

The chest was shown on the main evening news programme of the Vox commercial television channel, which said a German family had brought it to the Berlin office of weekly news magazine Der Spiegel, where police secured it.
Vox said serial numbers on the back of the chest matched those in an inventory made when the room was intact.

The mosaic found last week depicts two couples relaxing in a garden landscape and was traced by police to a notary in Bremen who had been given it for safe-keeping while the son of a wartime soldier tried to sell it.
The Amber Chamber was dismantled and removed from an imperial palace near St Petersburg, then called Leningrad, by German troops in 1941.
It was last seen in 1945 in Koenigsberg, which was then a city in East Prussia and now, renamed Kaliningrad, lies in a Russian enclave surrounded by Poland and Lithuania.
